Since the turn of the 20th century.
So I set out to learn what a Y is and what was essential for the new space to truly be a YMCA.
I visited WISE across Canada including municipally built facilities in Calgary that are among the biggest WISE in the world.
And communities where municipalities and YMCA's work closely together.
While every YMCA looks different, they all share common characteristics.
They focus on safety, especially child safeguarding.
They build long-term relationships, not simply deliver services.
And they adapt to meet the changing needs of their communities, supporting physical, health, mental health, social connection and belonging.
What that looks like varies.
In Winnipeg, an elder and resident helps build understanding and connection through cultural teachings and reconciliation programs.
In left bridge, flexible community space serves older adults during the day and youth in the evenings.
In Regina, the Y delivers YMCA, the evidence-based mental wellness program that helps people manage stress and anxiety.
And here in Saskatoon, we partner with the community to deliver our programs, including learn to golf for children and small steps for big change.
A program helping individuals at risk are developing type 2 diabetes through fitness, education and support.
These examples are all different, but they reflect the same principle.
A YMCA is not simply a building operator.
A YMCA is a community building organization that uses recreation wellness and human connection to strengthen communities.
The foundation that makes this model work is membership.
Membership is not just a revenue source. It creates relationships, stability and belonging.
A day pass user access is a facility. A member becomes part of a community.
Members return week after week and year after year, healthy habits form, friendships developed, programs grow around their needs.
Membership also creates sustainability.
A flexible revenue allows organizations to maintain facilities, introduce new programs, provide financial assistance and respond to changing community needs.
To make the model successful, however, the facility must be designed with the amenities needed to attract and retain members.
Fitness space is not simply another amenity. It is what drives membership growth and helps support aquatics youth programming, inclusion initiatives and subsidized access.
The stronger the membership base, the greater the community impact.
This is why the discussion around capital investment matters.
The Y has advocated for additional investment, not because we need a bigger building, but because we want a facility that will meet the needs of Saskatoon's.
A Saskatoon's needs for decades to come.
Our current YMCA facility is expected to close before 2030, including its six-lane pool.
If the new facility only replaces those six lanes, Saskatoon gains little additional aquatic capacity, despite significant population growth.
Similarly, the proposed YMCA investment could expand the fitness center and ideally support an indoor walking track.
It was one of the highest ranked amenities identified during the city's public engagement.
The top four were swimming, swimming lessons and fitness and a weight space.
The reality is that a $95 million budget requires trade-offs, not every priority can be included.
But these facilities are built once every 15 to 20 years and are expected to serve communities for generations, cost matters, but so does value.
Today's decision is about more than selecting an operator.
It is about choosing the operating model that will best serve Saskatoon for the next 30 to 40 years.
One model primarily delivers a defined set of services and requires ongoing subsidy,
and the YMCA model creates incentives to grow, innovate, adapt, and reinvest as community needs evolve.
This is what makes the YMCA YMCA.
It is a commitment to belonging, inclusion, innovation, and community impact.
A facility designed to support a strong membership model will create both long-term financial sustainability and long-term community benefit.
Saskatoon deserves a facility that does more than just maintain services.
It deserves a facility built for the future, one that grows alongside its community.
That's the opportunity before council today.
